Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: UnitedHealth is a dominant, well-known company but not a Rule Breaker: it leads a mature industry, its brand is unpopular, and its stock has lagged the market over five years. It fails Gardner's tests for an emerging industry and a hard-to-copy, beloved advantage.
summaries.buffett: It is a large, understandable franchise with strong cash generation and a long record of profits, and Berkshire disclosed a stake in 2025. But earnings fell sharply in 2024-2025, regulatory and legal risks are high, and the price of about 22.6 times trailing EPS offers no obvious margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value its scale and integration but worry about inverting the risks: dependence on government payments, DOJ investigations and public hostility. It is a good business, though not one with few ways to fail.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would call it a stalwart in a turnaround, with insiders buying in 2025 and earnings rebounding in 2026. However, a P/E of about 22.6 against 10-13% expected EPS growth gives a PEG above 1, and it is anything but overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Its sales force and Optum services are strong and management is investing in AI tools, but growth has stalled in 2026 and margins fell for three years. It partly fits Fisher's quality points but not his preference for sustained above-average growth.
summaries.graham: It is large, has paid dividends since 1990 and has been profitable for over ten years, with EPS up about 120% from 2015 to 2025. It fails Graham's price tests: about 22.6 times average earnings and P/E times P/B near 77.
summaries.thiel: UnitedHealth is a scale incumbent in a regulated market, not a company with a ten-times-better proprietary technology or a secret. It scores well on distribution and durability but poorly on Thiel's questions about technology and unique opportunity.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a fair price; UnitedHealth offers rebounding earnings and a 6% free-cash-flow yield but roughly flat 2026 revenue. It fits as a value recovery more than a compounding growth story.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are accelerating and estimates are rising after three guidance raises in 2026, which suits Druckenmiller's focus on change at the margin. But policy and legal uncertainty make a large concentrated bet hard to justify.
summaries.smith: It has strong cash conversion and a defensive market, but low operating margins (about 5%), high debt and recent earnings declines fall short of Terry Smith's high-return, high-margin quality standard.
summaries.greenblatt: With a trailing earnings yield near 6% on enterprise value and a return on equity around 15% that leans on debt and goodwill, it would rank as middling under the Magic Formula.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, talented and honest management and reinvestment runway. UnitedHealth has scale and experienced leadership, but its returns have fallen, integrity questions remain and reinvestment opportunities are being trimmed.
summaries.pabrai: It fits Pabrai's idea of a temporarily troubled good business where permanent loss looks unlikely, but the price no longer reflects the deep pessimism of mid-2025, so the heads-I-win odds are less compelling.
summaries.wood: UnitedHealth is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's platforms; it is an incumbent that disruptive health-tech players hope to challenge. It does not fit Cathie Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and barriers to entry; UnitedHealth meets the cash and dominance tests but is exposed to government policy and is less predictable than his ideal.
summaries.sleep: Its scale could in theory let it share savings with customers, but it is not known for scale-economies-shared behaviour and its regulatory position is weaker than a decade ago, so it fits Nick Sleep's approach only partly.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and companies solving big, painful problems; health coverage is such a market, but UnitedHealth is a mature incumbent rather than an early-stage disruptor.
summaries.nash: UnitedHealth fails most of Nash's hard filters: revenue growth below 10%, operating margin near 5%, more debt than cash, and major regulatory threats. Its Nash scorecard totals about 60, below the 75 threshold.

momentum.evidence: Shares were up about 17% year to date by Oct 13, 2026 versus about 14% for the S&P 500, but only about 8% over one year versus 17.5% for the index, and down about 11% over three months (24/7 Wall St.).

g4.evidence: Stephen Hemsley, architect of Optum, returned as CEO in May 2025 and bought about $25 million of stock; Berkshire Hathaway disclosed a stake in 2025, but leadership turnover and DOJ probes cloud the picture.

g6.evidence: Commentators mostly call UNH a beaten-down recovery story rather than overvalued: it trades at about 17 times 2027 consensus EPS and 26 analysts average a $477.72 target versus a $395.62 price.

simple.evidence: The idea (collect premiums, pay for care, run pharmacy and clinics) is simple, but medical-cost reserving, risk adjustment and government reimbursement rules make results hard for a generalist to forecast, as the 2024-2025 surprise showed.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from 2015 ($157.1B) to 2025 ($447.6B) and diluted EPS grew from $6.01 to a peak of $23.86 in 2023, but EPS then fell to $15.51 (2024) and $13.23 (2025).

integrity.evidence: Management is now candid about the 2025 mistakes and the dividend and buybacks are disciplined, but the company suspended 2025 guidance in May 2025, faces DOJ criminal and civil Medicare investigations, and was criticised over executive stock sales before the 2024 probe disclosure.

b6.evidence: UnitedHealth built Optum through hundreds of acquisitions (Change Healthcare, LHC, Amedisys, physician groups), a pattern of empire-building it is now partly reversing by exiting markets.

roic.evidence: Trailing net income of about $15.9 billion on $104.1 billion of equity is roughly a 15% return, but debt is $74.3 billion (41.7% debt-to-capital) and goodwill-heavy acquisitions dilute returns on total capital.

fcf.evidence: 2025 operating cash flow of $19,697M less $3,622M capex gave $16,075M of free cash flow, more than the $12,056M net income; in the first nine months of 2026 operating cash flow was $25,087M.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded big acquisitions, yet the share price ($395.62) is only about 3% higher than five years ago, so retained capital has not added matching market value recently.

safety.evidence: At $395.62 the stock trades at about 22.6 times trailing diluted EPS ($17.52) and a simple DCF at 12% gives about $347 a share, so there is no clear margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 19 times 2026 adjusted EPS guidance (at least $20.50) and about 17.5 times 2027 consensus ($22.61) is reasonable if management delivers its 13-16% long-term EPS growth target, but expensive if margins stall.

mu5.evidence: It depends heavily on government payment rates, risk-adjustment rules, antitrust tolerance of its insurer-plus-provider model, and medical-cost trends; DOJ investigations and PBM reform are live threats.

reinvest.evidence: Optum Health, Optum Rx and AI tools offer reinvestment room, but the company is shrinking value-based care and Medicare Advantage footprints in 2026 and returns on acquisitions have been mixed.

ly2.evidence: A stalwart turned turnaround: a giant, steady compounder hit by the 2024-2025 cost shock that is now rebuilding margins.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E is about 22.6 versus analysts' expected EPS growth of roughly 10-13% for 2027 ($22.61 vs at least $20.50).

runway.evidence: Ageing Americans and rising health spending give steady growth, but 2026 revenue is roughly flat ($336.4B vs $334.4B for nine months) and consensus 2027 revenue is $462.8B, only about 3% above 2026.

ly7.evidence: Insiders including CEO Hemsley (about $25 million) bought heavily in May 2025, and diluted shares fell from 961M (2020) to 902M (Q3 2026); no comparable 2026 insider buying has been reported.

ly8.evidence: It is one of the most widely followed US stocks, covered by 26 analysts and a Dow Jones component.

fi2.evidence: Management is launching AI-first Optum Insight products and AI tools now used by over 40% of employed clinicians, but much of its innovation historically came through acquisitions.

fi3.evidence: UnitedHealth does not report a separate R&D figure, so the payoff from its technology spending cannot be measured directly.

fi4.evidence: It runs the largest US health-insurance sales operation and Optum Rx has won external clients so that over half its membership is now outside UnitedHealthcare, with retention in the high 90s.

longterm.evidence: In 2026 management chose to give up about 935,000 Medicare Advantage members and exit unprofitable value-based care markets to restore margins, a long-term discipline call, but its strategy has long been driven by quarterly EPS targets.

gr1.evidence: FY2025 revenue was $447.6 billion and market value about $355 billion, among the largest US companies.

ni10.evidence: It has been profitable every year from 2016 through 2025, with 2025 net earnings of $12,056M, its lowest in several years.

gr4.evidence: UnitedHealth began paying annual dividends in 1990 and has paid quarterly dividends since June 2010 (company investor site).

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $6.01 in 2015 to $13.23 in 2025, up about 120%, despite the 2024-2025 decline.

gr6.evidence: The price of $395.62 is about 22.6 times average 2023-2025 diluted EPS of $17.53 ($23.86, $15.51, $13.23).

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 22.6 times price-to-book of about 3.4 (equity of $104.1B on about 898M shares) is roughly 77, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: It has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals; its edge is scale and integration.

timing.evidence: Medicare Advantage rates for 2027 were raised and medical cost pressure is easing in 2026, helping recovery, but the market for its core products is not being newly created.

th3.evidence: It grew by consolidating an already-large insurance market and acquiring health services businesses, not by dominating a small niche first.

th5.evidence: It has huge distribution: employer brokers, Medicare agents, state Medicaid contracts and Optum's direct relationships with health systems.

durable.evidence: Demand for health coverage is permanent and its scale will persist, but policy changes (MA payment cuts, PBM reform, possible forced break-up of payer and provider units) could reshape its position over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Its integrated Optum strategy was distinctive in the 2010s but CVS, Cigna and Humana have since copied it.

trend.evidence: It benefits from an ageing population and is deploying AI in claims and clinical work, but it is not a leading beneficiary of a platform shift like AI or cloud.

dr1.evidence: Adjusted EPS rose from $2.92 to $4.69 in Q3 2026 after $6.38 in Q2, guidance has been raised three times to at least $20.50, and 2027 consensus EPS rose from $20.97 to $22.61 over 90 days.

dr2.evidence: Optum Health margin repair (6-8% target by 2028) and MA repricing could make 2027-2028 look better, though management already guides to the low end of 13-16% EPS growth for 2027.

dr4.evidence: Higher interest rates help investment income on its float, and health spending is little affected by the economy, but government budget pressure on Medicare and Medicaid is a headwind.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include a 2027 outlook before year-end 2026, 2027 Medicare Advantage rate increases, star ratings, and resolution of the DOJ investigations.

dr7.evidence: Regulatory and legal uncertainty (DOJ probes, PBM reform, MA policy) argues against a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: It does not report gross margin; its operating margin was only 4.2% in 2025 (about 5.3% trailing), typical of a low-margin insurer and PBM.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $22.8 billion (9M 2026 operating cash flow $25,087M plus Q4 2025) against a $355 billion market cap is about a 6% yield, attractive for a recovering market leader.

gb2.evidence: Trailing earnings from operations of about $23.9 billion against an enterprise value of about $401 billion is an earnings yield near 6%, middling for the Magic Formula.

pa2.evidence: The 2024-2025 surge in medical costs, Medicare Advantage rate cuts and the V28 risk model are a cyclical, partly fixable setback; margins are already recovering, with the Q3 2026 medical care ratio at 88.4% vs 89.9% a year earlier.

pa4.evidence: As the largest US health company with $447.6 billion of revenue, positive free cash flow and a 2.35% dividend yield, permanent loss of capital looks unlikely even if the recovery is slow.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing, though it uses AI internally.

wo2.evidence: Its costs are dominated by medical claims, which rise rather than fall with volume.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market grows steadily with health spending, not many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: Results depend heavily on government payment rates and policy, and interest rates affect investment income.

ns1.evidence: Optum Rx passes most drug rebates to clients and scale lowers unit admin costs, but it is not known for systematically sharing scale savings with customers like Costco or Amazon.

ns4.evidence: Its scale and data should endure, but rivals like Humana are gaining Medicare share and regulatory risk is higher than a decade ago.

va2.evidence: Paying for and coordinating health care for about 48 million insured Americans addresses a huge, painful problem.

tn1.evidence: It rides the ageing-population and rising health-spending trend, but it is an established insurer retrofitting AI, not a company built for a new trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees an insurer in trouble; it is also a large health-services, pharmacy and data company (Optum's 2025 segment revenue was $276 billion before eliminations), though that is widely known.

tn3.evidence: It is a US mega-cap, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: revenue grew every year through 2025 and it is profitable, but debt ($74.3B) exceeds cash ($28.5B), which is normal for a large insurer.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive, but debt has exceeded cash and short-term investments in every recent quarter (e.g. $74.3B vs $28.5B at Sept 30, 2026).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew only 0.6% in the first nine months of 2026 and consensus FY2026 revenue of $448.4B is about 0.2% above 2025.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth near 0.5% plus a trailing free-cash-flow margin of about 5% is roughly 6, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: Over the latest nine months revenue rose 0.6% while costs (revenue minus earnings from operations) fell about 0.9%, lifting earnings from operations from $18.6B to $23.5B.

tn9.evidence: It fails several instant kills: more debt than cash, an operating margin of about 5% (below 20%), and revenue growth below 10%.

tn10.evidence: It faces DOJ criminal and civil investigations into Medicare Advantage practices, PBM reform proposals and antitrust scrutiny of Optum.

tn11.evidence: It provides health insurance, pharmacy benefits and care that help employers, governments and individuals pay for and get medical care, charging premiums and service fees; customers choose it for its national network and integrated services.

tn13.evidence: Total about 60 of 130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 0, short interest 10 (1.8%), institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year 2020-2025, but operating margin fell from 8.7% to 4.2%, free cash flow fell from $20.1B (2020) to $16.1B (2025), and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage was 4.7x in 2025 ($18,964M / $4,002M) and liabilities are about 2.1x equity, but the current ratio was 0.79 ($90.6B / $114.9B) and goodwill-heavy assets fail the 2x test.

tn18.evidence: Hemsley has a strong long record and bought about $25 million of shares in the open market in May 2025, but he has been CEO again only since 2025 and is not the founder.

tn20.evidence: It beat estimates in Q2 2026 ($6.38 vs $4.92) and Q3 2026 ($4.69 vs $4.14), but missed badly in 2025, including suspending guidance in May 2025.

tn21.evidence: Red flags include declining operating margins in 2023-2025, DOJ investigations into Medicare billing, a long acquisition spree, and scrutiny of insider stock sales in 2024.

tn22.evidence: It has $447.6 billion of revenue, positive earnings and cash flow, and buys back rather than sells shares.

tn24.evidence: At $395.62 the price implies sustained high-single-digit growth with stable 5% FCF margins, more than the roughly flat revenue the company is delivering in 2026.

tn25.evidence: Using about 8% trimmed growth (3-year average 11.4%), a 5.2% three-year average FCF margin, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate, net of $45.8B net debt, value is about $347 a share, below $395.62.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 17.5 on 2027 consensus ($22.61) is above Cigna's roughly 8x and implies a PEG around 1.4-1.7 given expected EPS growth of 10-13%.

team.evidence: CEO Stephen Hemsley built Optum during his 2006-2017 tenure and returned in May 2025 with a new CFO, Wayne Deveydt; the team has delivered three 2026 guidance raises, but it is not a founder-led, world-class-innovator team and lost credibility in 2024-2025.
